overview.body:
**Ambikā** ​(*ambika*) — ‌Divine Mother ‌· epithet ​of Pārvatī/Durgā ​· multi-armed ​with lion ​— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Divine ‌Mother, Power, ​Protection". The ‌name means ​"Mother; epithet ​of Pārvatī/Durgā, ​the multi-armed ​goddess with ​lion"[^1].

**Ambikā** ‌is ​the Mother ‌who takes ​up arms. ‌As an ​epithet of ‌Pārvatī and ​Durgā, she ‌is the ​gentle parent ​become warrioress: ‌multi-armed, riding ‌or attended ‌by a ​lion, and ​invoked against ‌the demons ​who threaten ​cosmic order. ‌Her name ​means 'mother', ​but in ‌cult ​it means ‌'mother who ​fights for ​her children'.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as **Ambikā** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at [ambikā.com](https://xn--ambik-jwa.com). ​The restoration ​preserves at ‌least one ‌distinctive feature ‌— a ‌diacritic or ​a distinctive ‌letter — ​that the ​ASCII form ​loses, and ‌exactly ​one historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places ​the name ​in Tier ​1. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *ambika* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.
Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī), Translated by C. Mackenzie Brown, 500.

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari ​as **अम्बिका**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Mother; ​epithet ​of Pārvatī/Durgā, ‌the multi-armed ​goddess ​with lion"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form *ambika* ‌survives ​only because ‌the early ​domain-name ​system could ​not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Ambikā** recovers ​the vowel ‌length ​of the ​original directly ‌in the ‌address ‌bar. The ​restoration preserves ​at ‌least one ​distinctive feature ​— a ‌diacritic ​or a ​distinctive letter ‌— ​that the ‌ASCII form ​loses, ​and exactly ​one historically ​valid Unicode ‌restoration ‌exists, which ​places the ‌name ​in Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

‌- **a** ‌→ **A** ​— ‌Initial a, ​capitalized
- ​**m** ​→ **m** ‌— Ma
​- **b** ​→ ​**b** — ‌Ba
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ​— Short ‌i
​- **k** ‌→ **k** ​— Ka
‌- ​**a** → ‌**ā** — ‌Long ​ā (macron)

​The canonical ​temple for ​this ‌name is ‌served at ​**ambikā.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/əmbiˈkaː/** ​— ​Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**am-** — ‌Short ​a ‌plus ​labial ​nasal m, ​a ​soft ​opening.
‌- ​**-bi-** — ‌Voiced ​labial ‌stop ​plus ‌short i.
​- ‌**-kā** ​— ​Voiceless ‌velar ‌stop plus ‌long ​ā, ​the ‌feminine ​ending.

For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ‌'um-bee-KAH' ​— ​the ​final syllable ​is ‌long ‌and ​carries ‌the weight ​of ​the ‌name.

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ​of ‌the ​name:

​- ​**Sanskrit** — ‌अम्बिका ​(Ambikā), ​'the ​mother'

‌Ambikā means ​literally ​'little ​mother' ‌or ​'dear mother', ‌an ​affectionate ‌epithet ​that ‌became a ‌name ​of ​the ​Goddess ​in her ‌protective, ‌warrior ​form.

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.
Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī), Translated by C. Mackenzie Brown, 500.

domains.body:
**Ambikā** ​is ‌the Mother ‌who ​takes ​up ​arms. ​As an ​epithet ‌of ​Pārvatī ​and Durgā, ‌she ​is ‌the ​gentle parent ‌become ​warrioress: ​multi-armed, ​riding ​or attended ​by ‌a ​lion, ‌and invoked ​against ‌the ​demons ‌who ​threaten cosmic ‌order. ​Her ​name ‌means 'mother', ‌but ‌in ​cult ​it means ‌'mother ​who ​fights ‌for ​her children'.[^1]

​### ‌Divine ​Motherhood

‌The maternal ​face ​of ​the ​Goddess, ‌compassionate and ‌inexhaustible.

​### ‌Warrior ​Protection

She ​wields ‌weapons ‌against ‌demons to ‌defend ​devotees ‌and ​restore ​dharma.

### ​The ‌Lion

​Her ​vehicle and ​symbol ‌of ​sovereign, ​ferocious ​maternal power.

‌### ​Multi-Armed ‌Might

​Each arm ‌carries ​a ‌divine ‌weapon gifted ​by ​the ​gods ​for ‌the destruction ‌of ​evil.

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.

mythology.body:
Ambikā's ​mythology is ‌not separate ‌from that ​of ​Pārvatī and ​Durgā; it ​is one ​mask ‌of the ​Great Goddess, ​the one ‌who becomes ​a ‌mother to ​the cosmos ‌and a ​warrior ​to its ​enemies.[^1]

### ​Ambikā as ​Pārvatī ‌(Epithet)

In ​the Shiva ‌Purana, Pārvatī ​is ‌called Ambikā ​when she ‌appears as ​the ‌divine consort ​and mother. ​The name ‌softens her ‌into ‌maternal affection, ​yet the ​same goddess ‌can ​assume the ​ten-armed form ‌of Durgā ​when ​demons threaten ‌the gods.[^2]

​### The ‌Slayer ​of Demons ​(Devi Mahatmya)

​When the ​buffalo-demon ‌Mahiṣāsura overthrows ‌the gods, ​the Goddess ‌emerges ​from the ​combined tejas ‌of the ‌gods. As ‌Ambikā/Durgā ‌she rides ​a lion ‌and destroys ​the ​armies of ​demons, restoring ‌cosmic order ​through ​martial motherhood.

​### Worship ‌across India ​(Cult)

​Ambikā is ​worshipped in ‌temples across ​Gujarat, ‌Rajasthan, and ​Maharashtra, often ‌as a ​local guardian ‌goddess ‌and healer. ​Her shrines ​are frequented ​by ​women seeking ‌protection for ‌children and ​family.

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.
Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī), Translated by C. Mackenzie Brown, 500.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Ambikā ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Sanskrit name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ​would ‌take ‌recognizable ​forms: votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions ‌naming ‌अम्बिका, ‌sanctuary ‌or cult ​remains ‌tied ​to ​divine ​mother ‌and iconography ​matching ​its ​traditional ‌attributes ​(lion ​and trident ​(trishūla)). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sources.citation: Śiva Purāṇa, English translation by J. L. Shastri, 500.
Devī Māhātmya (Durgā Saptaśatī), Translated by C. Mackenzie Brown, 500.

meditation.body:
Ambikā ​teaches ‌that ‌motherhood ​is not ​passive. ​In ​her, ​the ‌womb ​and ​the weapon ‌are ​not ‌opposites ​but ‌complements: ​the ​same love ​that ​gives ​birth ‌will ​destroy ‌anything ​that ‌threatens the ​child. ‌This ​is ‌not ​a ​sentimental ‌goddess; she ‌is ‌a ​sovereign ​parent ‌whose ​tenderness ​has teeth.

‌For ​the ​devotee, ‌Ambikā ​is ‌the ​assurance ​that the ​cosmos ​has ‌a ‌mother, ​and ‌that ​the mother ​is ‌armed. ‌She ‌does ‌not ​promise ‌an end ​to ​struggle; ​she ‌promises ​that ​the ​struggle ‌is on ​the ​side ​of ‌order, ​dharma, ‌and ​life. To ‌call ​on ‌Ambikā ‌is ​to ​remember ​that protection ​can ‌be ‌holy ​rage.[^1]
